title: Uniqueness of Planet Earth
seo_title: Grade 11 General Science: Uniqueness of Planet Earth Worksheets (Strengthened SHS)
standard_code: Grade 11 General Science, Term 3: Earth and space science
standard_text: Uniqueness of planet Earth: Earth's position in the solar system and the habitable zone; the four subsystems (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere) and their interactions; the layers of the atmosphere. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, General Science, Term 3)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 General Science worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Term 3): the habitable zone, Earth's subsystems, the atmosphere, liquid water and life. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Earth is the only planet known to have life.
body_html:
How to think about it

Earth is the right distance from the Sun for liquid water, has an atmosphere rich in nitrogen and oxygen, a magnetic field that shields it from solar wind, and plate tectonics that recycle materials. These make it the only planet known to support life.

Earth has four subsystems: the geosphere (rocks and soil), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air) and biosphere (living things). They interact: rain (hydrosphere) erodes rocks (geosphere), plants (biosphere) add oxygen to the air (atmosphere).

Example

Why is Earth in the 'habitable zone'?

Liquid water

Answer: its temperature lets water stay liquid

Example

A volcano releases gases into the air. Which subsystems interact?

Rock and air

Answer: geosphere and atmosphere

Common mistakes

  • Thinking Earth is the only planet with an atmosphere.
  • Thinking the subsystems work separately.
  • Thinking the ozone layer is in the troposphere.

faq.q: Why does Mars not have liquid water on its surface now?
faq.a: It is colder and its atmosphere is too thin.

items.q: Which statement about energy and matter in the Earth system is correct?
c: matter flows in from the Sun
energy flows through the system from the Sun and out to space, while matter is mostly recycled
matter is lost to space quickly
items.e: Earth is close to a closed system for matter.

items.q: A large forest is cut down. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere and geosphere (more CO₂, more soil erosion)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: Glaciers melt quickly in a warm period. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the atmosphere (cooler temperatures for a year or two)
the atmosphere and geosphere (more CO₂, more soil erosion)
the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: More rainfall speeds up rock weathering, which removes CO₂ from the air over long times. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: What is residence time?
c: the average time matter stays in a reservoir
the time a river takes to reach the sea
items.e: Water stays in the atmosphere for about 9 days but in deep groundwater for thousands of years.

items.q: Which sphere includes all of Earth's water, including ice and groundwater?
items.e: Ice is sometimes called the cryosphere.

items.q: Mangrove roots trap mud along a coast. Which spheres interact?
items.e: Living things change the shape of the coast.

items.q: Warmer oceans evaporate more water, forming more low clouds that reflect sunlight and cool the surface. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Warming thaws permafrost, which releases methane, which causes more warming. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Rain falling on a mountain wears away rock and carries sediment to the sea. Which spheres interact?
items.e: Weathering and erosion link the spheres.

items.q: Earth is usually described as a closed system. What does this mean?
c: it exchanges energy with space but almost no matter
it exchanges lots of matter with space
it is not affected by the Sun
items.e: Meteorites and escaping gases are tiny amounts.

items.q: What does dynamic equilibrium mean for an Earth system?
c: inputs are always larger than outputs
the system is always changing quickly
inputs and outputs balance so the system stays about the same even though matter keeps moving
items.e: A stable lake has inflows that balance outflows.

items.q: Drought kills plants, so less water evaporates from leaves, so less rain falls, making the drought worse. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Which sphere does the ozone layer belong to?
items.e: It is in the stratosphere.

items.q: What is a reservoir (store) in an Earth system model?
c: a place where matter is held for a time, such as the ocean or the atmosphere
items.e: Fluxes move matter between reservoirs.

items.q: Warming melts sea ice, exposing dark ocean that absorbs more sunlight, which causes more warming. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: Coral reefs die from warm water. Which other Earth system is most directly changed, and how?
c: the geosphere and hydrosphere (coasts erode faster without reefs)
the hydrosphere and biosphere (a lake forms, fish migration is blocked, sediment is trapped)
items.e: A change in one sphere spreads to others.

items.q: More CO₂ makes some plants grow faster and take up more CO₂. What kind of feedback is this?
items.e: It partly offsets the rise in CO₂.

items.q: Why do scientists use models of Earth systems?
c: because models are always exactly right
to simplify complex systems so they can be explained and predictions tested
items.e: All models have limitations.

items.q: A hotter Earth gives off more infrared energy to space, which cools it down. What kind of feedback is this?
c: a feedback that only affects rocks
items.e: Positive feedback makes the change bigger; negative feedback makes it smaller.

items.q: What did the Miller–Urey experiment show?
c: simple organic molecules such as amino acids can form from gases and an energy source

items.e: It modeled early Earth conditions.

items.q: What are stromatolites?
c: layered structures built by mats of cyanobacteria that trap sediment
items.e: Living stromatolites grow at Shark Bay, WA.

items.q: What are banded iron formations (BIFs)?
c: rocks with layers of iron oxide formed when oxygen reacted with dissolved iron in the oceans
items.e: Most were laid down 2.5–1.8 billion years ago.

items.q: What is a mass extinction?
c: the loss of a large proportion of species in a geologically short time
the slow extinction of one species
items.e: There have been five major mass extinctions.

items.q: What is the evidence from fossils that life has changed over time?
c: fossils are found only in young rocks
all fossils are the same age
different rock layers contain different fossils, with simpler life in older layers
items.e: This is the principle of faunal succession.

items.q: What does this evidence tell us about early Earth: Moon rocks brought back by Apollo?
c: The Moon formed from material similar to Earth's, likely after a giant impact.
The early solar system had many large impacts.
Oxygen began to build up in the oceans and air.
Earth had solid crust and probably liquid water very early.
items.e: Old materials record early events.

items.q: Why are cyanobacteria called 'the organisms that changed the world'?
c: their oxygen-releasing photosynthesis transformed the atmosphere and oceans
items.e: They still produce much of Earth's oxygen.

items.q: What are red beds, and what do they show?
c: land sediments colored by iron oxides, showing oxygen was present in the atmosphere
items.e: They appear after about 2.2 billion years ago.

items.q: Why did early Earth's oceans contain lots of dissolved iron?
c: there was almost no oxygen, so iron stayed dissolved
items.e: Oxygen later made it precipitate as iron oxide.

items.q: Which gases made up most of Earth's early atmosphere?
c: carbon dioxide, water vapor and nitrogen, from volcanic outgassing
items.e: There was almost no free oxygen.

items.q: Which change in living things caused this: Coal deposits formed and atmospheric CO₂ dropped.

Huge swamp forests grew and were buried before they decayed.
Cyanobacteria began photosynthesis in the oceans.
items.e: Match the cause in the biosphere.

items.q: What is coevolution of life and Earth?
c: life and Earth never affect each other
life changes Earth's systems, and those changes in turn affect how life evolves
items.e: Oxygen from life allowed animals to evolve.

items.q: How did the evolution of land plants affect the atmosphere about 400 million years ago?
c: they removed large amounts of CO₂ and helped cool the climate
items.e: Plants also sped up rock weathering.

items.q: Which change in living things caused this: Soils formed and rock weathering sped up, pulling CO₂ from the air.

Plants spread onto land and their roots broke up rock.
Huge swamp forests grew and were buried before they decayed.
Corals and shelled plankton built skeletons from calcium carbonate.

items.q: What is an open system?
c: a system that exchanges only energy
a system that exchanges both matter and energy with its surroundings
items.e: A river basin is an open system.

items.q: Cyanobacteria began photosynthesis in the oceans. How did this change Earth's systems?

Wetlands and ponds formed, changing water flow.
An ozone layer formed that blocks harmful UV.
Oxygen built up in the oceans and atmosphere.

items.q: Which four spheres make up the Earth system model?
c: crust, mantle, outer core and inner core
items.e: Matter and energy move between the spheres.

items.q: What is a flux in an Earth system model?
c: the rate at which matter or energy moves between reservoirs
items.e: Evaporation is a flux from ocean to atmosphere.

items.q: How did land plants change Earth's systems?
c: they increased weathering, built soils and drew down carbon dioxide
they added carbon dioxide to the atmosphere
items.e: Forests also changed the water cycle.

items.q: What is a negative feedback loop?
c: a change that triggers effects that reduce the original change
a feedback that always warms Earth
a change that is made larger by its effects
items.e: Negative feedback tends to stabilize a system.
